[ALUSI-FULL:v16p59/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو هريرة | reports | A sound-graded report from Abu Hurayra says Zakariya was a carpenter.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p59/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Zakariya’s name has five forms: long and short forms read in the Seven, two forms of Zakari, and Zakar like qalam; it is foreign.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p59/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الراغب | reports | Nidāʾ ordinarily means raising and projecting the voice, but Raghib allows it to mean any sound or any sign indicating something.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p59/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Here nidāʾ means supplication privately made and unheard by people, perhaps in the middle of the night; secrecy better protects sincerity and avoids ostentation, reproach, and harm from his relatives.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p59/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Secrecy need not mean a quiet voice: he could call loudly where nobody could see or hear him; alternatively hiddenness is a figure for sincerity and lack of ostentation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p59/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الكشف | reports | Al-Kashf regards the phrase as a figure with literal secrecy also intended: concealment itself was desired, while sincerity was the chief purpose.
[TABATABAI:19:1-3/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The surah’s purpose is warning and glad tidings, illustrated through the stories of prophets granted divine friendship, prophethood, truthfulness, and sincerity. | mentions 19:97
[TABATABAI:19:1-3/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The surah contrasts humble, grateful predecessors with descendants who abandon devotion for desire and error, while allowing repentant believers to return to the blessed path.
[TABATABAI:19:1-3/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Stories serve as examples for a general division into the blessed, the erring, and repentant believers, followed by their respective reward and punishment; the surah rebuts denials of resurrection, divine offspring, and worship of idols. | mentions 19:58
[TABATABAI:19:15/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The Qur'an calls Zechariah prophet and recipient of revelation, servant, righteous, elect, and guided; it recounts his prayer for a child after witnessing Mary's worship and provision. | mentions 6:85, 6:87, 3:37, 3:38-41
[TABATABAI:19:3-8/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The time clause attaches to God’s mercy; nida ordinarily means calling aloud, unlike private supplication, but can be hidden when spoken where people cannot hear.
[TABATABAI:19:3-8/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The description of the call as hidden is compatible with speaking aloud in private, as Zechariah later leaves the prayer niche to address his people.
[TABATABAI:19:3-8/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · بعضهم | reports | Some say Zechariah used the word calling because his sins and poor condition made him feel distant from God, like someone fearing punishment.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p496/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The prophets in Adam’s, Noah’s, and Abraham’s lines preached monotheism, prayer, and zakāh, but their followers turned to polytheism, abandoned the rites, and followed innovations and desires.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p496/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The Prophet is urged to persevere against their hostility and is given glad tidings of success.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p496/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The adversaries mistake worldly success for proof of their truth; it is only respite until the truth is conclusively conveyed and they have no excuse when seized.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p496/r5] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Jesus and Mary are prominent because Christians and Jews secretly supported Quraysh; the Qur’an exposes the People of the Book to show they cannot support a truthless cause.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p496/r6] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The Zacharias story introduces Mary’s story and counters Christians who treat Jesus’s miraculous birth as proof of his divinity.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-surah-maryam-19:p500/r5] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Zacharias probably made the prayer while in iʿtikāf at the Temple; private prayer is the foremost etiquette and aids acceptance because it is free of pretension.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:19:2/r2] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Quiet, humble, pleading prayer best fits its etiquette; Zakariya feared his relatives would fail to lead the community and spread God's religion, so he sought a virtuous, capable, just successor from himself and Jacob's line, never despairing of God.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p612/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | Khafiyah derives from concealment, while khīfah derives from fear; the latter appears in 7:205, unlike the خفية of 7:55 and 19:3. | mentions 7:205
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p612/r5] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | In Arabic, ḥaḍara means being present or existing, the opposite of absence, and does not necessarily mean coming to a place.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p791/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | Maryam’s night framing suits the hidden prayer: the secrecy of the whisper evokes the concealment of night.
[STUDYQURAN:19:2/r4] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | Zachariah’s secret supplication signals sincerity; loud prayer can suggest hypocrisy or seeking human notice. | mentions 4:142, 7:55
[STUDYQURAN:19:2/r5] STUDYQURAN · IK | reports | A low voice is especially favored by God.
